title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 3
paragraphs: When Michael Ivanovich returned to the study with the letter, the old prince, wearing spectacles and a shade over his eyes, was sitting at his open bureau with screened candles, holding a paper at arm's length, and reading in a somewhat dramatic pose his manuscript—his "Remarks" as he called it—which was to be sent to the Emperor after his death.

When Michael Ivanovich entered, there were tears in the prince's eyes, stirred by the memory of the time when the paper he was reading had been written. He took the letter from Michael Ivanovich, put it in his pocket, folded up his papers, and called in Alpatych, who had been waiting a long time.
The prince had a list of things to be bought in Smolensk, and walking up and down the room past Alpatych, who stood by the door, he gave his instructions.
"First, writing paper—do you hear? Eight quires, like this sample, with gilt edges... it must be exactly like the sample. Varnish, sealing wax, as on Michael Ivanovich's list."
He paced back and forth for a while and glanced at his notes.
"Then hand to the governor in person a letter about the deed."
Next, bolts for the doors of the new building were needed, and they had to be of a special design the prince had created himself, and a leather case had to be ordered to keep the "will" in.
The instructions to Alpatych took over two hours, and still the prince didn't let him go. He sat down, sank into thought, closed his eyes, and dozed off. Alpatych shifted slightly.
"Well, go, go! If anything else is needed, I'll send after you."
Alpatych went out. The prince went back to his bureau, glanced into it, fingered his papers, closed it again, and sat down at the table to write to the governor.

It was already late when he rose after sealing the letter. He wanted to sleep but knew he wouldn't be able to, and that his most depressing thoughts came to him in bed. So he called Tikhon and went through the rooms to show him where to set up the bed for that night.

He walked about examining every corner. Every place seemed unsatisfactory, but worst of all was his usual couch in the study. That couch was dreadful to him, probably because of the oppressive thoughts he'd had while lying there. It was unsatisfactory everywhere, but the corner behind the piano in the sitting room was better than the rest: he had never slept there yet.
With the help of a footman, Tikhon brought in the bedstead and began setting it up.
"That's not right! That's not right!" cried the prince, and he himself pushed it a few inches from the corner, then closer in again.
"Well, at last I've finished. Now I'll rest," the prince thought, and let Tikhon undress him.

Frowning with the effort of removing his coat and trousers, the prince undressed, sat down heavily on the bed, and seemed to be thinking as he looked disdainfully at his withered yellow legs. He wasn't really thinking, but only putting off the effort of lifting those legs and turning over on the bed. "How hard it is! Oh, if only this labor would end and You would release me!" he thought. Pressing his lips together, he made that effort for the twenty-thousandth time and lay down. But barely had he done so when the bed seemed to rock back and forth beneath him, as if it were breathing heavily and jerking. This happened nearly every night. He opened his eyes just as they were closing.

"No peace, damn them!" he muttered, angry without knowing at whom. "Ah yes, there was something else important, very important, that I was saving for when I'd be in bed. The bolts? No, I told him about those. No, it was something—something in the drawing room. Princess Mary was talking some nonsense. Dessalles, that fool, said something. Something in my pocket—can't remember..."
"Tikhon, what did we talk about at dinner?"
"About Prince Michael..."
"Quiet, quiet!" The prince slapped his hand on the table. "Yes, I know—Prince Andrew's letter! Princess Mary read it. Dessalles said something about Vitebsk. Now I'll read it."

He had the letter taken from his pocket and the table—on which stood a glass of lemonade and a spiral wax candle—moved close to the bed. Putting on his spectacles, he began reading. Only now, in the stillness of the night, reading by the faint light under the green shade, did he grasp the letter's meaning for a moment.
"The French at Vitebsk—in four days' march they could be at Smolensk; maybe they're already there! Tikhon!" Tikhon jumped up. "No, no, I don't need anything!" he shouted.

He slid the letter under the candlestick and closed his eyes. And there rose before him the Danube at bright noon: the reeds, the Russian camp, and himself a young general without a wrinkle on his ruddy face—vigorous and alert—entering Potemkin's brightly colored tent, and a burning sense of jealousy of "the favorite" stirred in him now as strongly as it had then. He recalled every word spoken at that first meeting with Potemkin. And he saw before him a plump, rather sallow, short, stout woman—the Empress Mother—with her smile and the words of her first gracious reception of him, and then that same face on the funeral bier, and the confrontation he'd had with Zubov over her coffin about his right to kiss her hand.
"Oh, let it be sooner, sooner! Let me get back to that time and be done with all this present! Sooner, sooner—and let them leave me in peace!"
